name: RightStart Mathematics
line: RightStart is taught by a parent with an abacus and card games. AMP places, checks and schedules review itself.
description: AMP vs RightStart Mathematics: an abacus, card games and a parent who teaches every lesson, or practice that places, checks and reviews on its own.
verdict: RightStart Mathematics is a homeschool program built on the Cotter Abacus and more than 300 card games, and for one young child it costs less [3][4][14]. The adult leads every lesson from a manual [7]. AMP teaches at the problem, checks and explains every answer, finds the level in each part of math, and brings old skills back on a schedule.

reasons.title: Teaching comes with every problem, no lesson plan needed
reasons.body: A RightStart lesson is led by the adult, with the abacus and other materials, from a manual that guides the teacher day by day [7]. A parent reviewer notes that the manual tells the parent what to say. She also reports reading that some people dislike the amount of teacher involvement, though she did not find it too much [16]. AMP teaches at the problem instead: a one-step hint, a written lesson with a worked example, and worked steps after every answer. Math still happens on a day no one can sit down to teach.

reasons.title: Placement comes from the child's own answers
reasons.body: RightStart's free placement test is a 2 to 3 minute online questionnaire about what the child can already do, and it gives one starting level [9]. AMP places the learner from their own answers in the first 24 problems, with a separate level in each of 14 strands of math, and keeps adjusting. A child sure of shapes and unsure of place value gets work at both levels in the same session.

reasons.title: Old skills return on a published schedule
reasons.body: RightStart practice comes through card games, with review worksheets kept to a minimum [7]. For students new to the second edition, review lessons open Levels B to F [10]. Its site argues that understanding reduces the need for review [8]. We found no schedule for when a skill comes back on the pages we read. AMP brings each learned skill back after 6 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and a month, mixed with other topics, and a miss starts the schedule over.

reasons.title: Learned means four of five right without help
reasons.body: RightStart names mastery as a goal and describes no test for when a lesson is learned [8]. Lessons follow the manual's day-by-day order, and the child advances at their own pace [6][7]. In AMP a skill is Strong when four of the last five answers are right without help, and an answer after a hint does not count. Two misses in a row send practice back to what the skill builds on, without waiting for an adult to notice.

reasons.title: One program from counting through precalculus
reasons.body: RightStart's own levels run A through H, and Levels G and H are its middle school course [10]. Its store also sells other publishers' algebra, geometry, precalculus and calculus books, which are different books and methods [1]. AMP covers counting through precalculus on one map of 336 skills and stops there. A learner who races ahead in one strand can move into any part of that map, with no new set of books and no new method.

reasons.title: Paper made for one learner
reasons.body: RightStart's worksheets come with the level bundle, as print or a PDF, the same published pages for every child [5]. AMP prints unlimited workbooks built from the learner's own record, with today's review and a challenge section, each with a worked answer key. Results entered from paper count toward the learner's level.

rows.price: Level bundle $99.25, or $109.25 with PDF worksheets [3]. Math Set of manipulatives $219.75, used at every level [4]. One-time purchase. Each extra child needs duplicate pieces [5].
rows.buyers: Families and tutors, through its own store [1][14]. A separate classroom edition for schools [1]. Returns within 60 days of receipt [10].
rows.range: Levels A to H instead of grades; G and H are middle school [6][10]. Higher courses are other publishers' books its store sells [1].
rows.start: A free 2 to 3 minute online questionnaire about what the child can do gives a starting level. Written tests for children switching programs [9].
rows.teaching: The adult teaches each lesson from the manual with the Cotter Abacus and other materials [7]. Optional videos for some levels [11][12].
rows.next: The next lesson in the manual's day-by-day order; the child advances at their own pace [6][7].
rows.mastery: Named as a goal and described as understanding. No stated rule for when a lesson counts as learned [8].
rows.review: Practice through card games, review worksheets kept to a minimum; review lessons open Levels B to F [7][10]. No schedule found on its pages.
rows.print: Print is the core: lesson manual, worksheets (print or PDF), appendix pages and card decks [4][5]. The same pages for every child.
rows.adult: Teach every lesson, play the practice games, and choose the starting level [7][9].
rows.reports: No progress reports or gradebook found on its home-school pages [1][7]. The adult keeps the record.
rows.evidence: One small Finnish kindergarten comparison: no significant difference from usual teaching [18]. A nine-child pilot with no group of similar children taught another way [19]. No Evidence for ESSA or WWC entry [20][21].

theirs: RightStart Mathematics comes from Activities for Learning, which describes itself as a family-owned business [2]. The curriculum grew out of Joan Cotter's doctoral dissertation, according to the company [17]. The home-school program runs in Levels A through H in place of grades [10], and a child begins at the level that fits [6]. Level A covers addition and subtraction to 10, place value to hundreds, money, clocks, measurement and basic geometry [5].

The adult leads each lesson from the manual, with the Cotter Abacus, a two-sided abacus grouped in fives and tens, and other materials from the Math Set [4][7]. Practice comes mostly through card games, more than 300 of them, with no flash cards [7][14]. The company's view is that math should be "95% is understood and only 5% memorized" [8].

Families buy a book bundle for each level and one Math Set that serves every level [3][4]. Around them sit optional game videos, video lessons for Levels C to F, online classes for Levels G and H, six apps for phones and tablets, and Spanish-language lessons [1][11][12][13]. RightStart reports first place in Practical Homeschooling's readers' poll for elementary math twelve years in a row [15].
credit: Hands-on materials. The Cotter Abacus and the Math Set's 23 items give a child something to hold for place value and facts [4][7]. A 2021 What Works Clearinghouse practice guide rates concrete and semi-concrete representations as strong evidence for elementary students who struggle in math [22]. AMP is on a screen, with only a few models a learner builds.
Games. More than 300 card games for practice, and six apps on iPhone, iPad and Android [13][14]. AMP has no games and no app in the stores.
A lower price for a young child, paid once: about $329 for Level A with the Math Set, then about $100 to $110 for each later level [3][4]. A 60-day return window [10].
Spanish-language lessons for several levels [1]. AMP is in English only.
Paper, wood and cards that need no screen or connection [5]. AMP needs a connection, though it prints workbooks.

theirs: Researchers at the University of Helsinki and the Niilo Mäki Institute in Finland compared RightStart with usual kindergarten teaching (Mononen, Aunio and Koponen, 2014) [18]. It was a comparison of classrooms, not a randomized trial: 38 children taught with RightStart and 32 taught as usual. The RightStart classes covered about 36 of the manual's 87 lessons. Both groups improved in counting, comparing numbers and addition facts. The study found no statistically significant difference between the groups after the lessons, or at a follow-up in first grade [18]. The authors call the sample small and ask that the results be read with caution [18].

A second paper from the same team followed nine children with specific language impairment taught with RightStart for seven months, 40 minutes two or three times a week, beside 32 typically developing peers [19]. The nine began with weaker skills. After the lessons their counting did not differ significantly from the peers', and in first grade they matched them in some skills and not in others. The authors call these encouraging signs. A foundation grant paid for the manipulatives. With no group of similar children taught another way, the pilot cannot show what RightStart itself caused [19].

RightStart Mathematics has no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse (checked November 2026) [20][21]. The company calls RightStart a research-based program. Its research page lists the two Finnish papers and a summary by Joan Cotter, and reports no results [17]. The 2021 What Works Clearinghouse practice guide rates concrete and semi-concrete representations as strong evidence for elementary students who struggle in math [22]. That supports the method; it is not a study of RightStart.
ours: Two of AMP's rules do what a printed program leaves to the adult. Mixed, spaced practice: in a randomized trial of 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, students who practiced this way scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [23]. Feedback that explains: across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, it averaged 0.49, against 0.32 for the correct answer alone and 0.05 for right or wrong only; effects were smaller in primary and high school settings, and these are averages, not a head-to-head trial [24]. AMP schedules the first and gives the second after every answer, even when no adult is at the table. We expect that to show in outcomes, and we have committed to measuring it in public.

AMP is new, and its own outcome studies have not run yet. They begin in 2027: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. Until then, the research behind each part of AMP is laid out in our report, and the code is public.

them: Choose RightStart if you want to teach math yourself, at the table, with an abacus and materials your child can hold.
Choose RightStart if you want fact practice through card games, off screens.
Choose RightStart if your child learns best in Spanish.
Choose RightStart if you want to pay once: about $329 for the first level and the Math Set, then about $100 a level.
amp: You can't teach a lesson every day, or would rather not, and still want math every day.
You want every answer checked and explained the moment it is given.
Your child is ahead in some parts of math and behind in others.
You want old skills to come back on a schedule without planning it.
You love RightStart's abacus lessons and want daily practice beside them that finds the gaps.

questions.question: Is AMP more expensive than RightStart Mathematics?
questions.answer: For one young child, yes (prices checked November 2026). RightStart's Level A bundle with PDF worksheets is $109.25 and the Math Set is $219.75, about $329 to start, then $99.25 to $109.25 for each later level [3][4]. AMP is $599 a year or $59 a month for the first child and $399 a year or $39 a month for each more; that buys placement, a chosen and checked problem every time, scheduled review and personalized workbooks from counting through precalculus.

questions.question: Can we use AMP alongside RightStart?
questions.answer: Yes. Keep teaching RightStart lessons with the abacus and use AMP for daily practice and review. AMP places the learner within the first 24 problems and keeps a level in each strand of math, so it does not need to know which RightStart level you are on.

questions.question: Does AMP use an abacus or hands-on materials?
questions.answer: No physical materials, and no abacus. AMP has a few on-screen models a learner builds, such as a peg board and a counter builder. If hands-on work with an abacus matters most for your child, RightStart is built around that [4][7].

questions.question: Has RightStart Mathematics been tested in studies?
questions.answer: One small Finnish kindergarten study compared it with usual teaching and found no statistically significant difference between the groups [18]. It has no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse [20][21].
